author: EDRi
title: Data retention is mass surveillance of people’s phone and internet activity
content:
In 2014, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) declared mass retention of internet traffic and location data as contrary to the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. Any proposal for a new EU instrument harmonising data retention must respect the boundaries of CJEU jurisprudence and uphold the rights to privacy, data protection and freedom of expression. Read more in EDRi’s new publication.

It is the legal requirement for internet service providers to retain metadata about their users beyond what is necessary for the provision of the service (e.g. billing or network optimisation and security purposes) and to keep it solely so that it can later be accessed by law enforcement bodies and intelligence services.

Metadata is data generated for the purpose of transmitting content in electronic communications services and networks. This includes mobile numbers of the sender and recipient, the time and duration of a call or an internet session, websites accessed, and the location of mobile devices. On a technical level, metadata is no longer needed once the transmission ends.

Metadata is very revealing about people’s private lives.

author: EDRi
title: EU governments call it ‘simplification,’ but their Data Omnibus deal considerably weakens our rights
content:
EU governments have agreed on their position on the Digital Omnibus, retaining changes that threaten fundamental rights to privacy and data protection. With negotiations moving to the European Parliament, MEPs must reject the proposed weakening of GDPR safeguards for AI and pseudonymised data, protect individual rights, and defend ePrivacy against new tracking exemptions. Genuine simplification should make our rights easier to exercise and enforce, not give companies more freedom to exploit our data.

When the European Commission presented its Digital Omnibus in November 2025, it promised to simplify Europe’s digital rules without weakening fundamental rights. Yet, as EDRi and others warned at the time, a majority of its proposals, particularly those regarding General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and ePrivacy, went far beyond reducing administrative burdens. They are part and parcel of a broad deregulatory wave that is devouring most of our rights and safeguards in the name of empty promises of competitiveness and sovereignty.

On 21 October 2026, EU governments agreed on their negotiating position, which has timidly corrected some of the Commission’s most questionable choices, but has mainly endorsed changes that could make exploiting personal data easier while making abuses even harder to challenge.

The result is a deal that weakens important safeguards and makes redress harder. There is also little evidence that weakening these protections will improve Europe’s competitiveness. Some changes may instead reinforce the advantages of Big Tech companies that already control and abuse enormous volumes of information about us and the people around us.

One of the most worrying changes concerns the use of personal data for AI.

The Council retained a dedicated provision, Article 88bis (Article 88c in the Commission’s proposal), explicitly recognising the possibility of relying on the GDPR’s ‘legitimate interest’ legal basis to use personal data when developing or operating AI systems. Under the GDPR, companies can already use this legal basis in certain circumstances, provided they demonstrate a legitimate interest, prove that processing is necessary, and establish that people’s rights do not override that interest.

The Council clarifies that AI development does not automatically constitute a legitimate interest and that existing conditions still apply. But if legitimate interests can already justify certain AI processing, why introduce a special provision?

The concern is that Article 88bis could tilt the legitimate interest assessment in favour of AI companies, giving preferential treatment to a vaguely defined set of technologies primarily owned by autocracy-supporting billionaires, regardless of the exact purpose for which our personal data is going to be used. As recent legal analysis explains, this risks changing how the existing balancing test between legitimate interest and data protection safeguards is applied, even without formally removing its requirements.

Companies could invoke this legislative endorsement to justify extensive data reuse, even when people never reasonably expected their information to be used for AI training. And who benefits most? The same dominant Big Tech corporations that have spent decades accumulating the most intimate information about billions of people.

The Council also retains an exception for sensitive personal data appearing incidentally in AI datasets (proposed Article 9(2)(k) and 9(2)), including information revealing health, political opinions or religious beliefs. Companies must try to avoid collecting and, where collected, remove such data, but may retain them under safeguards when removal proves technically impossible or requires manifestly disproportionate effort.

These conditions might look important, but risk turning difficulties in cleaning datasets into a justification for retaining highly sensitive information. In opaque AI systems, verifying whether such data have genuinely been isolated may often be impossible. In this regard we should bear in mind that companies are mandated to protect our data and rights, and technical choices should not determine how far our fundamental rights extend.

There is some, even if limited, good news. The Council has rejected the Commission’s attempt to rewrite the GDPR’s definition of personal data in Article 4.1 and dropped its proposed Article 41a, which would have allowed the Commission to specify when certain pseudonymised information could fall outside GDPR protection – which would likely be an unconstitutional move.

However, the underlying problem remains. Under a new Article 25a, pseudonymised data, where direct identifiers have been replaced or separated, could be considered non-personal for third parties unable to identify the individuals concerned.

Consider how information travels through websites, analytics companies, cloud providers and advertising intermediaries. Each organisation possesses different information and different capacities to link, single out or identify people, and very recent history is full of examples where re-identifying individuals from large datasets has been shockingly simple (it’s been done to Netflix film rating data, NYC cab drivers data, Australian health data, many more areas). The appearance of modern re-identification methods suggests that ‘even heavily sampled anonymized datasets are unlikely to satisfy the modern standards for anonymization set forth by GDPR and seriously challenge the technical and legal adequacy of the de-identification release-and-forget model.’

The Council position includes safeguards concerning processors and onward disclosures, and recognises that identifiability depends on the circumstances. Yet its approach still focuses heavily on whether an individual recipient can identify someone, rather than fully accounting for the wider context in which data are processed, linked and shared. The Court of Justice has called for a contextual, case-by-case assessment, not a general blanket assumption that pseudonymised data fall outside the GDPR whenever one recipient cannot identify someone.

This distinction has real consequences for rights protection: organisations could claim that information is non-personal, leaving people without the transparency and access rights needed to challenge its use, and supervisory authorities could face lengthy technical investigations just to establish whether the GDPR applies, particularly across complex data chains. Instead of simplifying compliance, the Council risks creating more uncertainty for everyone involved.

Several other changes proposed by the Commission have been taken on by the Council.

Companies would have more room to reject or charge for access requests considered abusive. Yet access rights are often the only way to uncover unlawful surveillance, discriminatory profiling or misuse of personal information.

The Council also retains a new exemption from GDPR transparency obligations for certain limited, low-risk processing activities, such as a sports club collecting members’ contact details to manage memberships or organise activities. Where organisations have reasonable grounds to believe that people already know who is processing their personal data and why, they may be exempted from providing the information normally required under Article 13 GDPR. Although considerably narrowed, the exemption still allows organisations to assume that people already have essential information about how their personal data are processed, rather than requiring them to provide it.

The Council also introduces a new exception allowing companies to process biometric data for identity verification without explicit consent or another existing exception to processing sensitive data foreseen in the law, provided the data or means of verification remain under the person’s ‘sole control.’ While this includes safeguards, the concept of sole control remains problematic, particularly when biometric verification becomes a condition for accessing essential services. It risks normalising the collection of highly sensitive personal information instead of encouraging less intrusive alternatives.

On automated decision-making, the Council preserves Article 22’s basic protection against certain solely automated decisions. However, it also clarifies that such decisions may be considered necessary for a contract even when a human could have made them. This gives companies greater room to justify automated decisions with significant consequences, while leaving human intervention primarily as a safeguard after the wrongful decision has been made.

The Council also adds useful methodological and ethical criteria to a new definition of scientific research in Article 4(38) GDPR. Nobody denies that commercially funded research can genuinely advance scientific knowledge, and should not be excluded simply because it has commercial applications. The concern, however, is that the proposed definition, combined with easier data reuse and reduced information duties for research, could allow activities such as routine product optimisation or commercial AI development without genuine scientific objectives or sufficiently rigorous methodologies to claim privileges intended for scientific inquiry.

One significant improvement is the Council’s decision to keep rules protecting access to our phones, computers and connected devices within the ePrivacy Directive, rather than transferring them to the GDPR. This preserves a crucial distinction, even more so when considering the attacks against this different fundamental right from so many different angles: ePrivacy protects the confidentiality of our devices regardless of whether the information accessed qualifies as personal data.

However, the Council introduces additional exemptions allowing access without consent, including audience measurement and measurement of contextual advertising.

Contextual advertising can provide a less intrusive alternative to behavioural ad targeting. But displaying an advertisement based on a webpage’s content does not necessarily require accessing information on someone’s device. Why, then, should measuring its performance justify a new consent exemption? It is true that the Council includes restrictions on profiling and reuse, but it still permits certain device-level data collection. In addition to this, its definition of contextual advertising also covers advertising based on a single search query. A query about abortion, debt or political beliefs can reveal highly sensitive information. Using one query instead of a longer browsing history does not automatically make the practice harmless.

The Council also allows companies to ask for consent again four months after someone refuses. This may reduce repeated requests, but people will still have to keep saying no.

Worse, it deletes the Commission’s proposed system of automated, machine-readable privacy signals. That proposal offered a genuinely rights-respecting way to simplify people’s lives: allowing them to express their tracking preferences once through browsers, operating systems, apps or connected devices, and requiring services to respect those choices. Instead, parts of the industry continue demanding more exemptions from consent to get rid of cookie banners. But eliminating annoying cookie banners should not mean eliminating the right to refuse tracking.

The Council has also introduced provisions that could trigger further revisions before the current negotiations have even finished.

Within six months, the Commission would have to report on GDPR Chapter IV, potentially reopening central accountability obligations for controllers and processors for discussion, particularly smaller organisations carrying out low-risk processing. It is true that smaller organisations deserve better support, but guidance, templates and better-resourced authorities can reduce compliance burdens without weakening safeguards. An organisation’s size is no reliable measure of the risks its processing creates for people.

The Council also requests a review of privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs) within twelve months, particularly regarding access to our devices. PETs can reduce risks, but technologies such as pseudonymisation do not necessarily prevent tracking, singling out, or harmful data reuse. Other references to PETs throughout the text raise similar concerns about using technical measures to justify narrower legal protections. One thing that was central to the essence of GDPR is that technical safeguards should help organisations meet their obligations, rather than become arguments for removing them.

The European Data Protection Board and European Data Protection Supervisor – all EU’s data protection watchdogs – have already warned that parts of the Digital Omnibus could reduce protection and increase legal uncertainty.

The Council has corrected some important problems, particularly concerning ePrivacy and the definition of personal data. But its position still makes extensive data reuse easier, weakens safeguards, and introduces legal exceptions that will generate further uncertainty.

The European Parliament must now address these problems. This means rejecting Article 25a’s approach to pseudonymised data, deleting the AI-specific Article 88bis and the new exception for sensitive data in Article 9(2)(k), and preserving meaningful safeguards for access, transparency and automated decision-making.

MEPs should also resist further consent exemptions under ePrivacy and restore legally binding, machine-readable privacy signals that allow people to refuse tracking without confronting endless cookie banners. With more than 1,800 amendments tabled, Parliament has an opportunity to prioritise genuine simplification that makes compliance easier for smaller organisations and rights easier to exercise and enforce.

Meanwhile, the promised competitiveness gains remain speculative. Giving companies that already control vast amounts of data more flexibility will hardly solve the EU’s dependence on dominant technology providers. The EU can simplify its digital rules without weakening fundamental rights. And if its competitiveness strategy increasingly depends on doing the latter, perhaps it is the strategy, rather than our rights, that needs reconsidering.

author: EDRi
title: EDRi-gram, 29 October 2026
content:
What has the EDRi network been up to over the past few weeks? Find out the latest digital rights news in our regular newsletter. In this edition: Celebrating end-to-end encryption, and the digital justice community in Europe and beyond

We’re still riding the high from October milestones showcasing the strength of our community. We had the pleasure of greeting many of you in person and online for #PrivacyCamp26 two weeks ago to discuss the origins of technology and how to pivot from conversations around “sovereignty” to meaningful, community-led self-determination. If you weren’t able to make it but you’re curious about the conversations, you can rewatch the livestream of some of the panel discussions.

Then, on October 21, we celebrated Global Encryption Day, highlighting end-to-end encryption as a crucial foundation to our right to safe and secure communication online and to life as we know it. Thanks to our members and partners, our message of protecting encryption was visible across several European capitals – from the metro trains of Prague to key landmarks in Berlin, Paris and Dublin with mobile “encryption trucks”. We also worked with European Sex Workers Alliance and Féministes contre le cyberharcèlement to raise awareness on the importance of safe and secure communications for sex workers as well as womens’ rights. author: EDRi
title: The internet should not demand constant self-defence: Fairness starts before the click
content:
A fair digital environment cannot – and should not – depend on everyone being permanently alert. Fairness must be built into the environment itself, not left to the skills of the people using it. In practice, that means rules, not appeals: cancelling must be as easy as subscribing, protection must be the default rather than a setting, and a system that detects a moment of weakness must not be allowed to act on it.

You open an app to answer one message. Twenty minutes later, you are still there. A video starts playing before you choose it. The next one follows automatically. A notification appears just as you are about to leave. Cancelling a subscription takes six steps. Signing up took one.

We often blame these experiences on bad habits, weak self-control or poor digital literacy. That lets the companies designing them off the hook. The truth is that many digital services are built to keep us watching, clicking, buying and sharing data. They test colours, wording, timing, rankings and notifications to see what hooks us most. They learn when we hesitate, when we are tired and what makes us stay. The resulting pressure is rarely accidental: it is the business model. author: EDRi
title: What the new Convention on Decent Work in the Platform Economy means for workers – and what’s next for implementation
content:
In June 2026, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) adopted a new Convention on Decent Work in the Platform Economy. Following in the footsteps of the EU’s Platform Work Directive, this Convention extends data protection rights for platform workers and contains innovative provisions to protect against the adverse effects of automated decision-making globally. But this is only the beginning. In this article, EDRi member Privacy International explores what’s next for ratification, implementation and the future of regulating worker surveillance in the EU and around the world.

By Privacy International (guest author) · October 29, 2026

On 12 June 2026, the International Labour Organisation (ILO) adopted Convention C193 on Decent Work in the Platform Economy. This is a landmark piece of legislation as the first global legally binding instrument regulating the platform economy and addressing the impact of technology on the world of work.

The Convention represents a significant step forward for workers’ rights around the globe. It reflects the growing consensus that digital platform workers need more adequate protection from abusive and exploitative employment practices. It also reflects the need to regulate the use of automated decision-making (ADM) in the workplace affecting platform workers, an issue Privacy International has developed a set of recommendations on.

author: EDRi
title: Draconian access block orders in Turkey
content:
Court orders to block access to X accounts in Turkey reached an unprecedented number in September 2026. In this blog, EDRi-member Alternatif Bilisim detail the crackdown on civil rights defenders and independent media in the country, and call on public authorities to reconsider block orders and protect fundamental rights.

By Alternatif Bilisim (guest author) · October 29, 2026

Court orders to block access to X accounts in Turkey reached an unprecedented number in September 2026, followed by the closure of T24, an independent news website. According to data from the EngelliWeb project of the Freedom of Expression Association (İFÖD), X blocked at least 1,270 accounts. In comparison, a total of 995 accounts were blocked in the entire year of 2025. In fact, the website of EngelliWeb, which tracks and documents online censorship in Turkey, was also blocked on 1 October 2026. Authoritarian measures and alarming levels of censorship in the country are increasingly eroding freedom of expression.

The common factor in all decisions related to access block orders is Article 8/A of Law No. 5651. author: EDRi
title: Surveillance in times of insecurity: a wicked and stupid strategy
content:
Sweden has been grappling with crime-related challenges in the past years. The difficulty to address violent crimes in cities notably has triggered extensive legislative reforms to increase surveillance and repression, including that of children. Tougher criminal penalties, widespread videosurveillance, mass electronic monitoring and government hacking are just a few examples illustrating the Swedish government’s attempt to counter public safety threats.

Sweden has been grappling with crime-related challenges in the past years. The difficulty to address violent crimes in cities notably has triggered extensive legislative reforms to increase surveillance and repression, including that of children. Tougher criminal penalties, widespread video surveillance, mass electronic monitoring and government hacking are just a few examples illustrating the Swedish government’s attempt to counter public safety threats.

However, this approach is not only misguided, as no evidence of its effectiveness exists, but also harmful to the fundamental right to personal integrity and thus to Swedish democracy. Furthermore, its impacts disproportionately fall on communities already marginalised and overpoliced.

author: EDRi
title: EDRi celebrates Global Encryption Day 2026
content:
On 21 October 2026, we celebrate the Global Encryption Day! Part of EDRi’s KISS campaign, we celebrate this day with our partners, online, in Brussels and in different European capitals.

On 21 October 2026, we celebrate the Global Encryption Day! Part of EDRi’s KISS campaign, we celebrate this day with our partners, online, in Brussels and in different European capitals.

A recent survey conducted by CDT Europe shows that across several European countries (France, Sweden, Poland, and Ireland), people consistently oppose measures that would compromise encrypted communication platforms. In France, 92% of respondents agree they have the right to have private conversations online, while the figure goes to 94% in Poland, 88% in Sweden and 93% in Ireland.

Encryption is great for protecting the way our messages travel on the internet. Through “end to end encryption”, anyone can make sure that the content of an online conversation can not be intruded upon, not even the server that facilitates the transmission.

This year, we have coordinated several campaign actions to celebrate encryption.

author: Chiara Miraglia
title: CPDP 20th international conference
content:
CPDP (“Computers, Privacy and Data Protection”) is a non-profit platform founded in 2007 by research groups at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel, the Université de Namur, and Tilburg University, later joined by INRIA and the Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research. Today, CPDP is carried by 20 academic centres of excellence from the EU, the US, and beyond. Based in Brussels, CPDP has become a world-leading multidisciplinary conference, convening a global community across research, policy, practice, civil society, and technology to engage with cutting-edge developments in privacy and data protection.

Organiser: 20 academic centres of excellence from the EU, the US, and beyond

The governance of the digital world is fragmented and faces difficult challenges. Technologies that shape our lives develop faster than the means – or even the will – to regulate them for the protection of privacy and other fundamental rights.

What We Owe the Future invites reflection on this contribution. Building on this, it looks ahead to what the future demands of us. What will the next twenty or more years need, and how should we help to build it? What do we owe to those who will inherit the world we shape today?
